## Part (a): Definition of curl zero in the sense of distributions

Let $U = (P, Q)$ be a (not necessarily continuous) vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $P, Q \in L^1_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^2)$. The **classical curl** is $\operatorname{curl} U = \partial_x Q - \partial_y P$, which may not exist pointwise if $U$ is not differentiable.

**Definition.** $U$ has **curl zero in the sense of distributions** if for every test function $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)$,

$$\langle \operatorname{curl} U,\, \varphi \rangle := -\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} Q\,\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x}\,dx\,dy \;+\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^2} P\,\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial y}\,dx\,dy \;=\; 0.$$

Equivalently, the distributional derivative $\partial_x Q - \partial_y P$, defined as the distribution acting on $\varphi$ via the above formula (obtained by integration by parts against smooth compactly supported $\varphi$), is the zero distribution.

---

## Part (b): Description of $\Gamma$

**Setup.** Let $U_1 = (a_1, b_1)$ and $U_2 = (a_2, b_2)$ be distinct constant vectors. Let $n = (n_x, n_y)$ be the unit normal to $\Gamma$ pointing from $\Omega_1$ into $\Omega_2$, and let $t = (n_y, -n_x)$ be the unit tangent to $\Gamma$.

**Computation of the distributional curl.** For any test function $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)$:

$$\langle \operatorname{curl} U, \varphi \rangle = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} Q\,\partial_x \varphi + \int_{\mathbb{R}^2} P\,\partial_y \varphi.$$

Splitting over $\Omega_1$ and $\Omega_2$ and integrating by parts on each piece (using that $P, Q$ are constant on each $\Omega_i$, so the volume terms vanish, and that $\varphi$ has compact support so the boundary terms at infinity vanish):

$$-\int_{\Omega_i} b_i\,\partial_x \varphi = -\int_{\partial \Omega_i} b_i\,\varphi\, n_x^{(i)}\,ds, \qquad \int_{\Omega_i} a_i\,\partial_y \varphi = \int_{\partial \Omega_i} a_i\,\varphi\, n_y^{(i)}\,ds.$$

On the interface $\Gamma$, the outward normal of $\Omega_1$ is $n$ and the outward normal of $\Omega_2$ is $-n$. All other boundary contributions vanish due to compact support of $\varphi$. Therefore:

$$\langle \operatorname{curl} U, \varphi \rangle = \int_\Gamma \bigl[(b_2 - b_1)\,n_x - (a_2 - a_1)\,n_y\bigr]\,\varphi\,ds.$$

Denoting the jump $[U] := U_2 - U_1 = (a_2 - a_1,\; b_2 - b_1) =: ([a], [b])$, this becomes:

$$\langle \operatorname{curl} U, \varphi \rangle = \int_\Gamma \bigl([b]\,n_x - [a]\,n_y\bigr)\,\varphi\,ds = \int_\Gamma \bigl([U] \cdot t\bigr)\,\varphi\,ds,$$

since $[b]\,n_x - [a]\,n_y = ([a], [b]) \cdot (n_y, -n_x) = [U] \cdot t$.

**The condition $\operatorname{curl} U = 0$ in distributions** requires $\langle \operatorname{curl} U, \varphi \rangle = 0$ for all $\varphi$, hence:

$$[U] \cdot t = 0 \quad \text{on } \Gamma.$$

Since $U_1 \neq U_2$, the jump $[U]$ is a **fixed nonzero constant vector**. The condition $[U] \cdot t = 0$ says that the tangent $t$ to $\Gamma$ is everywhere perpendicular to $[U]$, i.e., the **normal $n$ to $\Gamma$ is everywhere parallel to $[U]$**.

**Conclusion.** Since $[U]$ is a nonzero constant vector, the unit normal $n$ to $\Gamma$ must be constant (equal to $\pm\, [U]/|[U]|$) at every point of $\Gamma$. A smooth curve with constant unit normal is necessarily a **straight line**.

Therefore:

> **$\Gamma$ is a straight line whose direction is perpendicular to the jump vector $U_2 - U_1$.**

Equivalently, $\Gamma$ is a straight line with normal vector parallel to $U_2 - U_1$. The line can be located anywhere (its position is not constrained by the curl-zero condition—only its direction is), and $\Omega_1, \Omega_2$ are the two open half-planes on either side of this line.
